Field
FēLD
n. (rendering Hebrew sādeh and Greek agros)
From Old English feld, open country, level ground — the flat land as distinguished from the wooded and from the walled. The Hebrew sādeh carries the same contrast: it is what lies outside the city, outside the tent, outside the enclosure. This is why so much of Scripture's decisive action happens in the field. The field is where a man is unwatched, where the beast is wild, where the labour is done, and where there is no one to hear a cry.

Biblical Definition

The field is the open ground given to man for labour, and it is one of the plainest instruments of biblical theology. It is first the place of the curse: cursed is the ground for thy sake, thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth, and in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread. It is next the place of the first murder — Cain talked with Abel his brother, and when they were in the field Cain rose up against him — the field being precisely where there was no witness but God, whose answer was that the voice of his brother's blood cried from the ground. It is the place of providence toward the poor, since the law commanded that the corners of the field not be reaped and the gleanings not be gathered, which is how Ruth came to glean in the field belonging unto Boaz (Rut 2:3), and how a foreign widow was brought into the line of David and of Christ. It is the place of trust, for the lilies of the field neither toil nor spin and yet are clothed beyond Solomon. And in the Lord's own interpretation it becomes the world itself: “The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one” (Mat 13:38). To that He adds the harvest urgency — lift up your eyes, and look on the fields, for they are white already to harvest (Joh 4:35).

Webster 1828 Definition

The open ground outside the city and the enclosure, given to man for labour under the curse; in Scripture the place of the first murder, of gleaning mercy to the poor, of the tares among the wheat, and, in the Lord's own exposition, a figure of the world itself.

expand to see more

FIELD, n. 1. A piece of land inclosed for tillage or pasture; any part of the open country not covered with wood.

2. In Scripture, the open country, as opposed to the city and the tent. The beasts of the field; the herbs of the field; Cain and Abel were in the field. Genesis 4.

3. Ground appropriated to a crop, and hence a figure of the world in which the gospel is sown. The field is the world. Matt. 13.

4. The place of battle. The field of blood; to take the field; to keep the field. Hence also the plain of Megiddo and the valley of decision.

5. In the Mosaic law, the corners of the field and the gleanings were to be left for the poor and the stranger. Levit. 19; Ruth 2.

Key Scripture

Matthew 13:38 — "The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one;"

Ruth 2:3 — "And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers: and her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz, who was of the kindred of Elimelech."

John 4:35 — "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest."

Isaiah 5:2 — "And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes."

Modern Corruption

The parable of the field and the tares is regularly turned into a counsel of indifference — let everything grow, judge nothing — when the Lord's point is that final separation is certain and belongs to Him, not that difference is unreal.

expand to see more

Mat 13 is one of the most misapplied passages in the New Testament. Because the householder says, Let both grow together until the harvest, the parable is enlisted to forbid the church from marking any difference between the faithful and the false, and to make all discernment presumptuous. But the field in the parable is explicitly the world, not the church, and the Lord who forbids the servants to pull tares is the same Lord who commands the church to put away from among itself the wicked person, and who writes to Thyatira in anger because she suffered a false teacher to teach. The parable restrains vigilante uprooting in the world; it does not abolish discipline in the congregation. And its conclusion is anything but indifferent: the tares are gathered and burned, and the righteous shine forth as the sun.

A second corruption is agricultural and moral at once. The gleaning laws are read as an early welfare programme and then either dismissed as obsolete or annexed to a political scheme. What they actually establish is a particular kind of mercy: the owner does not harvest to the edge, and the poor must still come and glean. The provision is real, it costs the owner, and it preserves the labour and dignity of the one receiving. Ruth is not handed a portion; she works in the field from morning until evening, and Boaz commands that handfuls be let fall on purpose for her. The law is neither the modern entitlement nor the modern indifference, and it is worth recovering as it stands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sādeh is the open ground, the country outside the walls. Greek agros is the field or farm, and chōra the wider region, used of the fields white to harvest.

expand to see more

Hebrew sādeh (H7704) — field, open country; some 333 occurrences, from the beast of the field to the field of Machpelah that Abraham bought for a burying place.

Hebrew chēlqâh (H2513) — a portion or parcel of ground; the word for Naboth's inherited plot and for the parcel of a field that Jacob bought at Shechem.

Greek agros (G68) — a field, a farm, the country; the word of the field bought with the price of blood (Mat 27:7) and of the treasure hid in a field.

Greek chōra (G5561) — a region, a tract of country; used in Joh 4:35 of the fields white already to harvest.

Greek zizanion (G2215) — tares, darnel; a weed that closely resembles wheat until the ear forms, which is exactly why the householder forbids early uprooting.

Usage

"Of the open country under the curse: thorns and thistles (Gen 3:18); the beasts of the field; Cain and Abel in the field (Gen 4:8)."

"Of provision and gleaning: the corners of the field left unreaped (Lev 19:9); Ruth gleaning after the reapers (Rut 2:3)."

"Figuratively of the world and the harvest: the field is the world (Mat 13:38); the fields white already to harvest (Joh 4:35); the vineyard of the LORD of hosts (Isa 5:7)."
